Why This Licensing Model Exists
↑ top

The licensing model is intentionally structured to balance community adoption with long-term sustainability and enterprise readiness.

Specifically, it is designed to:

  • Remove ambiguity for developers
    You should always know what you can use, where, and under which conditions—without legal guesswork.
  • Reduce friction for legal and procurement teams
    Clear boundaries between open-source and commercial components make reviews faster and easier.
  • Withstand scrutiny during audits and acquisitions
    The structure and documentation are designed to hold up during formal security reviews, compliance checks, and M&A due diligence.
What Is Explicitly Documented
↑ top

Every component in the ecosystem clearly states:

  • what you can use,
  • how you can use it, and
  • what applies as your organization grows or changes ownership.

Nothing is hidden. Nothing is implied. There are no surprise obligations introduced later through transitive dependencies or unclear licensing boundaries.

An Authoritative Reference
↑ top

If you're evaluating for production, enterprise use, or long-term adoption, this page serves as the authoritative reference for licensing across the entire system.

It is written to be usable not just by engineers, but also by legal, security, procurement, and audit teams—without requiring additional interpretation or external clarification.

How to Read This Page
↑ top

Different components in the ecosystem serve different purposes and are therefore licensed differently.

  • Proprietary licenses grant usage rights but restrict modification and redistribution.
  • Dual licenses allow free development use while requiring a license for production.
  • Open-source licenses apply only to the code in the public repository and do not extend rights to proprietary dependencies.

References to audit review indicate areas that are commonly examined by auditors to confirm licensing clarity and compliance.

License Categories Used
↑ top

Proprietary Licenses

Used for core execution engines and premium runtimes where IP protection and commercial enforcement are required.

Dual Licenses

Used to balance free development access with enforceable production licensing.

Open-Source Licenses

Used for community frameworks, documentation, and developer tooling.

Component-Level Licensing
↑ top

Each license applies only to the specific component listed and does not grant rights to other parts of the ecosystem unless explicitly stated.

Open-source components do not convey rights to proprietary runtimes or engines, even when used together in the same application.

Extensible Behaviors, Controllers & Language Wrappers
↑ top

is designed to be extensible across both behavior and language boundaries. Behaviors, controllers, and language-specific wrappers are first-class extension points, and engineers are encouraged to build on top of the core.

Language wrappers (for example, framework- or language-specific packages such as /angular) extend /core by providing idiomatic APIs, metadata, or integration layers while delegating core execution to .

Because extensibility can introduce third-party or custom code, licensing obligations depend on how an extension is created, distributed, and governed. The categories below describe the supported models and how they affect licensing, audits, and acquisition reviews.

Extensibility Categories

  • -supplied — Maintained and distributed by the project.
  • Community-contributed (core / add-ons) — Created by the community and accepted into official repositories.
  • Language wrappers — Framework- or language-specific adapters that extend /core.
  • Third-party packages — Created and distributed independently outside control.
  • Internal-only implementations — Created and used privately within an organization.
  • Commercial extensions — Created by a company and sold or licensed separately.

licenses apply only to -controlled code and do not automatically extend to third-party, internal, or commercial extensions.

Key Clarifications

  • Language wrappers provide integration and developer ergonomics only and do not modify or replace the execution engine.
  • Wrappers must not imply ownership of trademarks or official endorsement unless explicitly approved.
  • Creating or distributing extensions does not change the licensing terms of the Engine or Vault.

This extensibility model enables to support multiple languages and frameworks while preserving clear IP boundaries, predictable licensing, and acquisition-safe review outcomes.

Runtime Enforcement for Commercial Extensions
↑ top

Commercial extensions may optionally integrate with the Vault licensing system to enforce runtime activation rules.

This mechanism allows third-party vendors to:

  • Declare that a Behavior or Controller requires a valid license
  • Perform custom validation logic (local or remote)
  • Allow or deny FeatureCell activation deterministically

Vault does not validate licenses. Vendors control validation logic. Vault enforces pipeline activation based solely on validation results.

If a licensed extension fails validation or times out, the associated FeatureCell is denied. If no extensions require licensing, activation proceeds automatically.

Acquisition & Audit Considerations
↑ top

The ecosystem is designed to be compatible with standard enterprise acquisition and due-diligence processes.

  • No copyleft licenses are used.
  • No GPL, AGPL, or SSPL dependencies are included.
  • Proprietary licenses include assignment provisions.
  • Open-source components use permissive licenses.
Trademarks, Copyright & Brand Assets
↑ top

In addition to software licensing, the ecosystem includes product names, trademarks, logos, and branded assets that are protected separately from source code.

These protections exist to prevent confusion, misuse, or misrepresentation of official projects and are standard for commercial developer platforms.

Trademarks

The following names are considered trademarks or pending trademarks of the project and may not be used to imply endorsement, affiliation, or official status without permission:

Use of these names in third-party projects, forks, or distributions must avoid brand confusion and should follow standard open-source trademark guidelines.

Logos & Visual Identity

The logo and related visual assets are protected brand assets. They may not be used in derivative works, commercial offerings, or redistributed materials without explicit permission.

Copyrighted Works

Documentation, website content, diagrams, examples, and non-code materials are protected by copyright unless explicitly stated otherwise.

Open-source licenses apply only to the source code within their respective repositories and do not grant rights to trademarks, logos, or brand identity.

Summary

  • Licenses govern code usage.
  • Trademarks govern names, branding, and identity.
  • Copyright governs documentation and non-code assets.

Formal registrations and enforcement may be applied as the ecosystem evolves.

Licensing FAQ
↑ top

Does using require a commercial license?

No. The framework is MIT-licensed. Commercial licenses apply only to specific proprietary components.

Can we use in production?

Yes, with a valid production license.

What happens if our company is acquired?

Commercial licenses are designed to be assignable during acquisition.

Are any copyleft licenses used?

No.
